subtitle: The table of contents proposed for Volume II. Every chapter on it is now published in the Volume II book
intro: Volume II pushes the method back toward the beginning of written time and fills in events that Volume I left out. The test for every chapter is the same: real people, writing dated records at the time, ideally from more than one side or culture, with later memoirs and chronicles flagged rather than passed off as diaries.

This is an outline, not research. The names below are the leads each chapter would start from, chosen because the records are known to exist; every date and claim still has to be verified the way Volume I was. Where a chapter's record is thin or one-sided, the note under it says so.
The parts run roughly in time order, so that read together with Volume I the two books form one long line from a pyramid logbook to the archives still collecting diaries today.

parts.title: Part One · Before the calendar turned (c. 2560 BC – AD 79)

chapters.title: The Pyramid Logbook
chapters.span: Giza and the Red Sea coast, c. 2560 BC
chapters.premise: The oldest diary we have: the logbook of an inspector named Merer, whose crew ferried limestone from the Tura quarries to Giza for Khufu's pyramid. Found in 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf, it records the work day by day, two columns to a day.
eyes: Merer — inspector of a boat crew (papyrus logbook, Wadi al-Jarf papyri)
The harbour accounts from the same cache — rations and shipments (administrative papyri)
Ankhhaf, Khufu's half-brother, named in the log as overseer at Giza (seen through Merer)
chapters.caution: Effectively a single vantage. Best used as a short prologue showing how old the dated, daily record is.

chapters.title: Written in the Stars
chapters.premise: Babylonian astronomers kept dated diaries of the sky for centuries and noted earthly events alongside it. Their tablets record the eclipse before Gaugamela, the battle itself, Alexander's arrival in Babylon, and, in 323 BC, the day 'the king died'.
eyes: Babylonian Astronomical Diaries — anonymous scholar-astronomers (dated cuneiform tablets, British Museum)
The Royal Ephemerides of Alexander's court — a day-book of his last illness (lost; survives only as quoted by Arrian and Plutarch, flagged)
Arrian, Plutarch, Diodorus — Greek and Roman historians writing centuries later (flagged as later histories)
chapters.caution: The only truly contemporary eyes are the Babylonian scribes; the Greek side must be marked as later reconstruction.

chapters.title: Ash at Misenum
chapters.span: Vesuvius and the Bay of Naples, AD 79
chapters.premise: Pliny the Younger's two letters to Tacitus describe the eruption from across the bay, and the buried towns preserve dated wax tablets, graffiti and contracts from the months before.
eyes: Pliny the Younger — at Misenum (letters written about 25 years later, flagged)
The Sulpicii business archive and Herculaneum tablets — dated legal documents of ordinary townspeople
chapters.caution: No true diary survives. Keep only if a strong second vantage can be assembled from the dated documents.

parts.title: Part Two · Plague, sieges and first contact (1348–1700)

chapters.title: The Great Mortality
chapters.premise: The Black Death seen at once from the papal court, a Tuscan city, and the Islamic world: a natural first link in the epidemic thread that Volume I's last chapter follows to the present.
eyes: Louis Heyligen — musician at the papal court, dated letter from Avignon, April 1348
Agnolo di Tura — Sienese chronicler who buried his own children (chronicle with personal lines, flagged)
Ibn al-Wardi — Syrian scholar's 'Essay on the Report of the Pestilence', written in Aleppo before he died of it in 1349
Gabriele de' Mussi — notary of Piacenza (treatise; flagged)
Ibn Khatima and Ibn al-Khatib — physicians in Andalusia (treatises, 1349)
chapters.caution: Mostly letters and chronicles rather than diaries; every eye needs a form tag.

chapters.title: The Last Days of Constantinople
chapters.premise: A Venetian ship's doctor kept a day-by-day diary of the siege from inside the walls, while Greek, Latin and Ottoman writers recorded the same weeks from the court, the Church and the Sultan's camp.
eyes: Nicolò Barbaro — Venetian ship's surgeon inside the city (diary)
Leonard of Chios — Genoese archbishop, dated letter of August 1453
George Sphrantzes — Byzantine courtier (chronicle written later, flagged)
Tursun Beg and Kritoboulos — Ottoman-side historians (later histories, flagged)
Cardinal Isidore of Kiev — dated letters after his escape
chapters.caution: Barbaro is the anchor; the Ottoman side has no diary, only histories.

chapters.title: First Contact
chapters.span: Caribbean, Mexico, the Pacific and Europe, 1492–1522
chapters.premise: From Columbus's first landfall to the return of Magellan's ship, with Europe's reactions in between, including a German painter who saw Moctezuma's gifts in Brussels.
eyes: Christopher Columbus — the 1492 log (survives only in Las Casas's abstract, flagged)
Hernán Cortés — dated letters to Charles V (Cartas de relación)
Antonio Pigafetta — journal of Magellan's circumnavigation, 1519–1522
Albrecht Dürer — diary of his journey to the Netherlands, August 1520, describing the Aztec treasures
Nahua authors — the Annals of Tlatelolco (written about 1540s, flagged) and later Nahuatl accounts
Bernal Díaz del Castillo — conquistador (memoir written decades later, flagged)
chapters.caution: The Indigenous record is real but not contemporary diary; the chapter must say so plainly rather than balance the sides falsely.

chapters.title: The Imjin War
chapters.premise: Japan's invasions of Korea seen through the war diary of Korea's great admiral, the refugee diary of a Korean gentleman, and the daily record of a Japanese Buddhist monk marching with the invaders.
eyes: Yi Sun-sin — Korean admiral (Nanjung Ilgi war diary, UNESCO Memory of the World)
Oh Hui-mun — Korean yangban refugee (Swaemirok diary, 1591–1601)
Keinen — Japanese Jōdo monk serving as army physician-chaplain (Chōsen Nichinichiki, 1597–1598)
Ryu Seong-ryong — Korean chief minister (Jingbirok, memoir, flagged)
Luís Fróis and Jesuit letters — European observers in Japan (dated letters)
chapters.caution: Needs careful handling of lunar dates and of atrocity material in Keinen's diary.

chapters.title: The Mandate Changes Hands
chapters.premise: The fall of the Ming and the Qing conquest seen by a Ming official keeping a diary in the south, a Korean prince's household held hostage by the Manchus who rode into Beijing with them, and a German Jesuit who stayed on in the capital.
eyes: Qi Biaojia — Ming official and garden-maker of Shaoxing (diary)
The Shenyang Diary (Simyang ilgi) — record kept by the household of Korean Crown Prince Sohyeon, hostage of the Qing
Johann Adam Schall von Bell — Jesuit astronomer in Beijing (dated letters and reports)
Zhang Dai — late-Ming essayist (memoirs written after the fall, flagged)
chapters.caution: Check exactly which months each record covers before committing; the Shenyang Diary's reach into Beijing must be confirmed.

chapters.title: Vienna Besieged
chapters.premise: The Ottoman siege of Vienna recorded by an Ottoman official's campaign diary from the Grand Vizier's camp, by defenders inside the walls, and by the Polish king who led the relief and wrote to his wife from the captured Ottoman tents.
eyes: The Ottoman master of ceremonies' campaign diary (published in German as 'Kara Mustafa vor Wien')
Johann Peter von Vaelckeren — Habsburg official inside the city (dated account of the siege)
Nikolaus Hocke — city secretary of Vienna (siege diary)
Jan III Sobieski — King of Poland (dated letters to Marysieńka, including 13 September 1683)
Silahdar Fındıklılı Mehmed Ağa — Ottoman palace official (chronicle, flagged)
chapters.caution: Ideal for side-by-side days; the Ottoman diary is a translation, so quotes must be avoided.

parts.title: Part Three · Earth, empire and hunger (1755–1883)

chapters.title: The Morning the Earth Moved
chapters.span: Lisbon and all of Europe, 1 November 1755
chapters.premise: An earthquake, tsunami and fire destroy Lisbon on All Saints' Day, and across Europe people record lakes sloshing, church bells ringing and a philosophical crisis.
eyes: Rev. Charles Davy — English clergyman in Lisbon (dated letter)
English and Hamburg merchants in Lisbon — dated letters home
Observers of the seiches in Britain and Scandinavia — dated reports to the Royal Society
Voltaire — dated letters of November 1755
Portuguese clergy and officials — dated reports to the crown
chapters.caution: Mostly letters; a good test of whether the format works without diaries.

chapters.title: The Year Without a Summer
chapters.span: Indonesia, Europe, North America and China, 1815–1817
chapters.premise: Mount Tambora erupts in 1815; a year later snow falls in June in New England, crops fail across Europe, Mary Shelley begins Frankenstein in a gloomy Swiss summer, and famine reaches Yunnan.
eyes: Thomas Stamford Raffles and British officers on Java — dated reports of the eruption
Thomas Jefferson — weather diary at Monticello, 1816
New England farmers and townspeople — diaries of the June snow
Mary Shelley and Lord Byron — journal and letters from Geneva, summer 1816
Li Yuyang — Yunnan poet writing of the famine (poems, flagged)
chapters.caution: The 1815 eruption itself has few eyewitness diaries; the chapter's strength is the global aftermath.

chapters.title: Opium and Gunboats
chapters.premise: The Chinese commissioner who destroyed the opium stocks kept a diary; so did British officers, American merchants and missionaries on the same coast.
eyes: Lin Zexu — imperial commissioner (diary)
Charles Elliot — British Superintendent of Trade (dated dispatches)
Robert Bennet Forbes and American merchants in Canton — dated letters
British naval and army officers — campaign journals
Chinese gentry and officials — dated memorials to the throne
chapters.caution: Lin's diary needs a reliable edition; check what is available in translation.

chapters.title: The Great Hunger
chapters.premise: The Famine recorded by a Wicklow landlady, an American Bible-reader walking the west, Quaker relief workers and officials — and the authentic voices separated from a famous suspect diary.
eyes: Elizabeth Smith — landowner's wife in Wicklow (diary)
Asenath Nicholson — American traveller and relief worker (dated narrative)
William Bennett — English Quaker, journal of relief work, 1847
Captain Arthur Kennedy and other relief officials — dated reports
Robert Whyte's '1847 Famine Ship Diary' — authenticity disputed (flagged, used only as a warning)
chapters.caution: Treat the disputed ship diary exactly as Volume I treats Defoe: named, not trusted.

chapters.title: The Black Ships
chapters.premise: Commodore Perry's arrival seen from the American flagship and from Edo, where a bookseller kept a diary of every rumour sweeping the city.
eyes: Matthew C. Perry — journal of the expedition
Samuel Wells Williams — the expedition's interpreter (journal)
Fujiokaya Yoshizō — Edo bookseller (Fujiokaya nikki, diary of news and rumour)
Kawaji Toshiakira — shogunate official (diary)
Japanese artists' dated broadsheets of the 'black ships' (flagged as prints)
chapters.caution: Lunisolar dates again; reuse the Heian chapter's conversion method.

chapters.title: Delhi, 1857
chapters.premise: The great rebellion of 1857 from inside Delhi, in the words of India's greatest Urdu poet and of Indian diarists in the city, set against British diaries from the siege of Lucknow.
eyes: Mirza Ghalib — poet in occupied Delhi (Dastanbuy, a Persian diary of 1857)
Munshi Jiwan Lal and Mainodin Hassan — Delhi officials (diary and narrative, translated 1898)
Katherine Harris — 'A Lady's Diary of the Siege of Lucknow' (1858)
Julia Inglis — wife of Lucknow's commander (diary)
British officers before Delhi — dated letters and diaries
chapters.caution: Violence on both sides must be handled with the same sobriety as Nanjing in Volume I.

chapters.title: The Sound Heard Round the World
chapters.span: Sunda Strait and the whole globe, August 1883
chapters.premise: Krakatoa's eruption logged by ship captains in the strait, heard 4,800 km away, and seen for months in blood-red sunsets recorded by diarists and scientists across the world.
eyes: Ship captains in the Sunda Strait — dated logbooks (e.g. the Charles Bal)
Dutch colonial officials at Batavia and Anjer — dated reports
The police chief of Rodrigues Island — report of the explosion heard across the Indian Ocean
Gerard Manley Hopkins — dated letters to 'Nature' on the sunsets
Royal Society observers worldwide — dated observations (Krakatoa Committee, 1888)
chapters.caution: Strong for 'one event, whole planet' — a natural sibling to the Year Without a Summer.

parts.title: Part Four · The long twentieth century (1936–1989)

chapters.title: Spain Divided
chapters.premise: The Spanish Civil War kept by a Republican president, a Soviet correspondent, foreign volunteers and soldiers on both sides.
eyes: Manuel Azaña — President of the Republic (diaries)
Mikhail Koltsov — Pravda correspondent ('Spanish Diary')
International Brigade volunteers — diaries held by the Abraham Lincoln Brigade Archives and others
Nationalist officers and civilians — published diaries
George Orwell — 'Homage to Catalonia' (memoir, flagged)
chapters.caution: Political framing is contested; keep each eye's own side visible and add no verdicts.

chapters.title: Moscow, 1937
chapters.span: The Soviet Union during the Great Terror, 1936–1938
chapters.premise: Ordinary and official Soviet diarists writing through the purges, some of whom were arrested because of their diaries, alongside a foreign ambassador's account of the show trials.
eyes: Diarists collected in 'Intimacy and Terror' (Garros, Korenevskaya, Lahusen), including Galina Shtange and Andrei Arzhilovsky
Mikhail Prishvin — writer (diary)
Sergei Prokofiev or other cultural figures — diaries (verify dates)
Joseph E. Davies — US ambassador ('Mission to Moscow', dated letters and journal)
Prozhito database — searchable diaries for single dates
chapters.caution: Translations are modern: digests only, no quotes.

chapters.title: The Sixth River
chapters.premise: The Partition of India through an Urdu writer's Lahore diary, the Viceroy's press attaché's diary, and dated letters from the leaders.
eyes: Fikr Taunsvi — Urdu writer ('The Sixth River: A Journal from the Partition of India')
Alan Campbell-Johnson — Mountbatten's press attaché ('Mission with Mountbatten', diary)
Jawaharlal Nehru and Muhammad Ali Jinnah — dated letters and speeches
The 1947 Partition Archive — oral histories (flagged as later testimony)
chapters.caution: Much of the human record here is later oral history; the chapter must label it clearly.

chapters.title: One Small Step
chapters.span: The Moon, Houston, Moscow and the world, July 1969
chapters.premise: Apollo 11 seen through NASA's own mission logs and transcripts, the diary of the head of Soviet cosmonaut training, and observatories and ordinary diarists who watched.
eyes: Apollo 11 crew — onboard transcripts and flight plan annotations (NASA, public domain)
Nikolai Kamanin — head of Soviet cosmonaut training (diaries)
Parkes Observatory and Honeysuckle Creek staff, Australia — dated logs of the television relay
Jodrell Bank — log of Luna 15 tracking during the same days
Diarists in archives such as the Deutsches Tagebucharchiv and the Great Diary Project
chapters.caution: A rare chapter where an official, public-domain record exists for the very centre of the event.

chapters.title: The Wall Opens
chapters.premise: The year the Eastern bloc came apart, from the diary of Gorbachev's foreign-policy aide in the Kremlin and from East Germans, Poles and Czechs keeping diaries as the borders opened.
eyes: Anatoly Chernyaev — Gorbachev's adviser (diary, published by the National Security Archive)
East German diarists — holdings of the Deutsches Tagebucharchiv
Mass Observation diarists in Britain — autumn 1989
Prozhito diarists in the Soviet Union
Polish and Czech dissidents — dated notes and samizdat diaries
chapters.caution: Many diarists are still living or recently died; privacy and copyright rules apply in full.
